title: CATL tests 350 Wh/kg battery for eVTOLs - electrive.com
content:
CATL has passed a demanding safety test with a battery system for electric aircraft. The manufacturer says thermal runaway did not spread to other cells after two adjacent cells were deliberately triggered simultaneously.
Image: CATL
Chinese battery manufacturer CATL has developed a battery system for passenger eVTOLs using prismatic cells with an energy density of 350 Wh/kg. According to CATL, it is the world’s first aviation battery system with prismatic cells at this energy density to pass the specified safety test.
According to a report by
CN EV Post,
two adjacent cells were deliberately triggered into thermal runaway simultaneously, both in the centre and at the corners of the battery pack. In none of the tests did the thermal runaway propagate to other cells. Such tests typically trigger only one cell, meaning that simultaneously triggering two adjacent cells significantly increases the test conditions. China’s aviation authority CAAC was involved in the manufacturing, inspection and testing of the cells and battery system. The stringent test is intended to lay the groundwork for meeting civil aviation safety requirements, although passing it does not constitute approval for commercial flight operations.
CATL says the battery system is ready for series production, with Chinese eVTOL developer AutoFlight as its first customer. The relationship between the two companies extends beyond a supplier agreement: in August 2024, CATL invested several hundred million dollars in AutoFlight
as a strategic investor
Energy density is particularly important for electric aircraft, as battery weight directly affects both range and payload. At 350 Wh/kg, CATL’s aviation cells significantly exceed the energy density of current EV batteries. At the same time, aviation imposes particularly stringent safety requirements, making the prevention of thermal propagation within the battery pack a key factor in its eligibility for certification.
CATL expands beyond electric vehicles
With aviation, CATL is expanding its battery technology into another application area. In its core vehicle battery business, the company has further strengthened its leading position: according to SNE Research, CATL supplied 242.7 GWh of batteries installed in electric and hybrid vehicles worldwide in the first half of 2026. That represents an increase of 25.3 per cent year-on-year and a global market share of 39.9 per cent.
Together with BYD, CATL now accounts for more than half of the global market
Aviation represents the next step in CATL’s diversification, which also includes battery solutions for electric ships. However, despite the aviation battery system being ready for series production, CATL must complete further approval and certification steps before it can be used to carry passengers in commercial operations.

title: How Gulfstream Collaborates with Suppliers on SAF Testing
content:
How Gulfstream Collaborates with Suppliers on SAF Testing
Prioritise Us
on Google
Gulfstream offers interior materials with lower environmental impact. Credit: Gulfstream
Gulfstream is working with fuel developers, engine makers and material suppliers to test sustainable aviation fuel and reduce carbon emissions
Business aviation manufacturers are testing new fuel types and design approaches to lower carbon output. According to the Aviation Environment Foundation, the
global aviation sector
accounts for approximately 2.5% of energy-related carbon dioxide emissions.
Gulfstream is one company attempting to reduce environmental impact through aircraft design and alternative fuel adoption.
The manufacturer has completed testing programmes and established partnerships to develop lower-emission operations.
Developing sustainable fuel partnerships
Gulfstream works with fuel developers and engine manufacturers to test
sustainable aviation fuel (SAF)
. The company has flown more than 3.5m nautical miles (6.5m kilometres) on SAF to date.
In July 2026, Gulfstream became the first business aviation company to complete a high-altitude flight test campaign with 100% SAF. The aircraft captured measurements of emissions and atmospheric conditions at altitudes typical for business aviation.
Mark Burns, President of Gulfstream, says: "As aviation continues its work in optimising environmental efficiencies, Gulfstream is focused on advancing solutions that deliver measurable impact today while shaping a more sustainable future for flight."
"This campaign reflects our strategy to lead with advanced technology, real-world testing and meaningful collaboration to better understand and reduce aviation's environmental impact."
Mark Burns, President of Gulfstream
The partnerships could show how fuel suppliers and aircraft manufacturers coordinate on testing new fuel types. SAF development requires collaboration across the aviation supply chain to reach commercial viability.
Aircraft design and materials sourcing
Gulfstream develops airframe, mechanical system and flight deck technologies to reduce fuel consumption. The company installs higher-efficiency winglets on aircraft to enable long-range flight with energy reductions.
The manufacturer partners with engine suppliers to set standards for flight performance on its aircraft. These partnerships could mean that component suppliers play a role in overall aircraft efficiency.
Gulfstream's design team works on sustainable interior finishes. The company uses third-party certified leathers or leather alternatives for reduced environmental impact.
Natural fibre textiles and countertops and veneers that meet international stewardship certification standards are available options. The material sourcing approach could show how manufacturers select suppliers based on environmental credentials.
Facilities and operational efficiency
Gulfstream aims to reduce water and energy usage and manufacturing waste. The company plans to achieve this through process improvements, energy conservation practices and energy efficiency initiatives.
Gulfstream has completed test flights with 100% SAF use. Credit: Gulfstream
The manufacturer has installed drought-resistant landscaping and energy-saving lighting, heating and cooling systems at facilities. Gulfstream currently has 2,379,728 total square footage of LEED and BREEAM certified buildings and facilities.
The certifications could mean decreased environmental impact and resource consumption across manufacturing operations. Facility design and energy management affect overall production efficiency.
Workforce development and local investment
Gulfstream has more than 13,000 employees in Georgia, US. The company has invested US$5m in education in the state.
The funding aims to strengthen talent, skills and innovation for
business aviation
. Mark says: "Each year, we invest US$5m in education through our Georgia partnerships, and we are proud to deliver our 2026 commitment today."
He adds: "Developing a strong local talent pipeline is essential to our future, and we are grateful for our educational partners who help prepare students with the skills and knowledge needed to succeed." The investment could show how manufacturers build workforce capabilities to support production requirements.

title: Inside Canada Goose's Supply Chain Sustainability Report
content:
Inside Canada Goose's Supply Chain Sustainability Report
Prioritise Us
on Google
Canada Goose is improving supply chain traceability. Credit: Canada Goose
Canada Goose is driving supply chain traceability across its operations, with an added focus of emissions reduction and waste avoidance
Canada Goose has cut its market-based Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 50% from its 2019 baseline. The luxury apparel company released its FY26 Impact Report, detailing Science Based Targets initiative-approved climate targets and 100% diversion of post-consumer global warranty waste from landfill in FY26.
The company manufactures most products in Canada, where it maintains oversight of production and material sourcing. This approach enables Canada Goose to track where products originate and how they are produced.
HUMANATURE NEXT GEN: Seek Out Sustainability
Material sourcing and traceability
According to the company,
improving transparency
across its supply chain remains central to its sustainability ambitions. Canada Goose expanded traceability during FY26 to better understand the environmental and social impacts of its materials.
The company collaborated with suppliers during FY26 to map upstream supply chains beyond Tier 2. This work increased visibility into material origins while identifying data gaps requiring further verification.
Manufacturing most products internally and sourcing the majority of materials directly provides greater visibility over operations. The company says these improvements support forced labour risk screening, preparations for future country-of-origin reporting requirements and more complete Scope 3 emissions reporting.
"Our latest Impact Report reflects both the progress we have made and how our approach to
sustainability is evolving
," Jeff Fitzpatrick, Head of Sustainability at Canada Goose, explained to Sustainability Magazine.
Jeff Fitzpatrick, Head of Sustainability at Canada Goose
"We have stronger data, deeper insight into our products and value chain and a clearer understanding of where our actions can have the greatest impact."
Supplier engagement and certification
Preferred Fibres and Materials accounted for 91% of materials used in Canadian manufacturing during FY26. All down was certified to the Responsible Down Standard and all wool suppliers signed the company's Non-Mulesed Wool Self-Declaration.
Canada Goose expanded its use of certified materials and recyclable packaging while strengthening supplier engagement through its traceability platform and social compliance programme. During FY26, 96% of leather purchased for offshore products was certified by the Leather Working Group.
Sea ice is becoming scarcer as temperatures rise in the Arctic. Credit: FloridaStock/Shutterstock
According to the company, 89% of materials were Bluesign approved and 98% were OEKO-TEX approved. The company is using supplier partnerships and environmental data to better understand biodiversity, water and ecosystem impacts linked to its priority materials and sourcing regions.
Supplier collaboration has also expanded the collection of primary emissions data. Logistics providers now represent 65% primary data coverage for transportation-related Scope 3 emissions.
Reverse logistics and circularity
Canada Goose is
embedding circularity
into manufacturing, product design and supply chain operations to reduce waste while extending product life. The approach focuses on designing products for longevity through durable construction, repair services and resale initiatives that keep garments in use for longer.
The Canada Goose Generations resale platform enables used products to be authenticated, restored and resold. More than 19,000 garments traded during FY26 through this platform.
The company has diverted more than 90,000 lbs of end-of-life products from landfill since 2020 through its reverse logistics partnership with Debrand. This partnership prioritises reuse and recycling before disposal.
"At Canada Goose, we're building something that will last and
sustainability is fundamental
to that ambition," says Dani Reiss, Chairman and CEO of Canada Goose.
Dani Reiss, Chairman and CEO of Canada Goose
"It shapes how we operate, the choices we make and the standards we hold ourselves to."
Manufacturing process improvements
Waste audits across Canadian manufacturing sites identified textile offcuts from fabric cutting as the largest source of waste. The company is piloting manufacturing process improvements aimed at reducing waste at source and supporting a broader circularity strategy.
Canada Goose completed life cycle assessments for every product manufactured during FY26. These assessments analysed impacts from raw material sourcing through manufacturing and global distribution.
The company has invested more than C$7m (US$4.96m) to electrify heating systems across its Canadian manufacturing facilities. This work replaced natural gas equipment with electric heat pumps powered by lower-carbon electricity grids in Ontario and Manitoba.
At one manufacturing site, heat generated by production machinery is now recovered to warm the facility. This approach reduced natural gas use and cut Scope 1 emissions at that location by 60%.
Long-term commitments
Jeff says Canada Goose is translating knowledge into practical decisions across climate action, responsible sourcing, nature,
circularity and ESG disclosure
and reporting. "Our goal is to reduce our environmental footprint, strengthen our operations and supply chain and build a more resilient business for the long term," he says.
Canada Goose plans to develop strategies to address nature-related risks identified through its ESG assessments. The company is continuing to strengthen partnerships focused on protecting ecosystems connected to its supply chain and long-term sustainability ambitions.
Masai Ujiri, Dallas Mavericks Team President and United Nations Sustainable Development Goals Advocate. Credit: NBA
"The UN Sustainable Development Goals remind us that businesses have a real responsibility to help build a stronger, more inclusive future for the next generation," says Masai Ujiri, Dallas Mavericks Team President and United Nations Sustainable Development Goals Advocate.
"It's encouraging to see Canada Goose align their
sustainability journey
with this intent, recognising that protecting the planet and creating social opportunity must go hand in hand."
Canada Goose has contributed nearly C$8m (US$5.67m) to Polar Bears International since 2007, supporting conservation research, climate education and Arctic habitat protection.

title: What is Heineken UK's Regenerative Agriculture Project?
content:
What is Heineken UK's Regenerative Agriculture Project?
Prioritise Us
on Google
Heineken’s strengthening its supply chain through regenerative agriculture practices
A new supply chain partnership will see almost half of Heineken malted barley in the UK come from regenerative agriculture sites, strengthening resiliency
Heineken
UK has launched a malting barley programme to help farmers in England and Scotland transition to regenerative farming practices at scale. The brewer produces more than 1.3 billion pints annually and supplies 80% of UK pubs.
Most of the barley used in Heineken UK's beer comes from British farms. The regenerative barley will be used across brands including Cruzcampo, Birra Moretti, John Smith's, Foster's and Amstel.
The first harvest is scheduled for 2026. Beer produced using these practices will reach market from 2027.
Heineken UK is partnering with malting companies Muntons and Boortmalt, barley merchant Cefetra and regenerative agriculture specialist Soil Capital.
The programme targets key barley-growing regions across East Anglia, the East Midlands, the Southeast, the Southwest, Fife and the Scottish Borders.
Climate Resilience for Barley Supply
Farmers participating in the programme receive customised support to implement methods including cover cropping, reduced soil disturbance and diverse crop rotations. According to Sonia Thimmiah, Corporate Affairs Director at Heineken UK, the initiative aims to build resilience into the supply chain.
Sonja Thimmiah, Corporate Affairs Director, Heineken UK
"We recognise the role that we can play in helping build a much more resilient and sustainable supply chain. And that's why we're investing in regenerative agriculture," says Sonia.
"The future of brewing depends on the future of barley."
Sonia referenced recent weather patterns affecting barley production. "You will have noticed the incredibly hot weather that we've been having lately. Reports this week say that more than half the country is in drought," she says.
"When we visited one of our farms a few weeks back, we were speaking to one of the farmers, and they were talking about the impact the low rainfall has had on spring barley."
Heineken’s Brew a Better World strategy is its long-term approach to doing business in such a way that it remains fit for the future
The future of brewing depends on the future of barley
Sonia Thimmiah
Corporate Affairs Director, Heineken UK
She noted that extreme weather events include flooding in areas such as Yorkshire. "Building that climate resilience is really key for us," says Sonia.
"British malting barley is at the heart of some of the UK's best-loved beers, so making it more resilient for the future matters."
Commercial support for farming transition
Farmers who join the programme receive additional payments for regenerative barley harvests. They also benefit from long-term agreements designed to reduce the financial risks associated with changing farming methods.
"This programme is about working with partners to make regenerative agriculture practical, scalable and commercially viable by strengthening soils and helping farms stay fit for the future," says Sonia.
"It is also an important contribution to Heineken's global Brew a Better World strategy and aims to protect water and nature as well as reduce carbon emissions."
Mark Tyldesley, CEO at Muntons, says the scale and collaboration between suppliers make the programme distinctive.
"We know from our work with growers that every farm is different and the transition to regenerative agriculture needs to be practical, commercially realistic and tailored to individual land," says Mark.
Mark Tyldesley, CEO at Muntons
"Through this partnership, we can help farmers identify the right steps for their business while supporting the long-term resilience of UK malting barley," he adds.
Independent verification of outcomes
The programme supports Heineken's global target of reaching net zero carbon emissions for Scope 1, 2 and 3 by 2040. Heineken UK is working with agronomist Soil Capital to certify improvements in agriculture and farming conditions.
Soil Capital manages independent measurement, reporting and verification using more than 30 indicators. These include soil resilience, water management, biodiversity and socioeconomics.
"All our programmes have an aspect of independent measurement and verification," says Sonia.
"[Soil Capital] are doing the measurements in the field so we can calculate the carbon emission reductions that come from what we're doing and how it contributes to the carbon reduction goals."
Sonia explained that other metrics are monitored to track improvements. "For the other metrics, we want to see a change and we want to see an improvement. It doesn't necessarily impact specific goals of ours, but we are really interested to see if this transition is really driving the benefits in terms of biodiversity and better water," she says.
"We already see some of it in soil health and through the other programmes, but we really need to do that on a consistent basis across all our programmes to make sure that the benefits we envisage are being delivered and to understand also where it doesn't."
Chuck de Liedekerke, CEO at Soil Capital, says monitoring regenerative processes could help secure buy-in from the agriculture community. "Soil Capital's first job is to make sure that we are at the forefront of what society expects in terms of outcomes," says Chuck.
Chuck de Liedekerke, CEO at Soil Capital
"Are these outcomes data-driven? Are they independently verified? And are they done in a way that also inspires trust with the farmer? Because the farmer has their own agronomic context."
Chuck emphasised that farmers cannot be asked to implement changes that conflict with profitability or crop production.
"This is what we do through data; we support farmers in adopting better farming practices. These farmers can then share data amongst themselves to make their transition more agronomically and economically relevant to themselves as well."
Farmers who enter the programme will implement practices annually. "The data that we capture through the software is then analysed and can be fed back to the farmers so that they can accelerate their transition in a way that makes the most sense for them."
Mark says interest from the farming community has been strong following earlier trials. "The uptake's been great. We've been working with farmers' groups across East Anglia, Yorkshire and Scotland for the last five years," he says.
"The people that we think are going to be supplying Heineken from crop 2026 are a mix of people who have been in those trials the last five years and absolutely love it and are advocates for the programme."
"And also people have come into it relatively recently having seen the results of the trials, and thought, actually this is something that I both want to do from a principal point of view, but also I'm comfortable with the level of risk in terms of yield, economic efficiency," says Mark.
Heineken UK brews over 1.3 billion pints each year
In April, Heineken appointed Simon Henzell-Thomas as Director of Global Sustainability after 14 years at IKEA.
Simon leads the integration of the company's 2030 Brew a Better World strategy into operations.
He highlighted collaboration as essential for sustainable programmes. "We know that regenerative agriculture practices can play an important role in strengthening soil health, improving environmental outcomes and building greater resilience in agricultural supply chains," says Simon.
"The programme announced by Heineken UK is a strong example of how we can work through strategic suppliers to support farmers in adopting more sustainable practices at scale."
Simon said the programme contributes to the company's sustainability ambitions. "It also makes an important contribution to our Brew a Better World ambitions, supporting our efforts to reduce carbon emissions while contributing to wider benefits for nature and water," he says.

title: Getting your teen a back-to-school e-bike? Don’t forget this cool-looking protective gear
content:
Micah Toll
| Aug 10 2026 - 8:46 am PT
Back-to-school season often means shopping for backpacks, notebooks, and maybe even a new ride. For a growing number of families, that ride is an electric bike.
And I’m all for it. Giving teenagers the freedom to get themselves to school, sports practice, or a friend’s house without needing a car is one of the best things e-bikes can offer. But just like we’d encourage a new driver to wear a seatbelt, young e-bike riders should be equipped with the right protective gear too.
A good helmet is the obvious starting point. And I’m glad to see that many parents get that part right. But after that, there’s another layer of gear that I think more families should consider for their e-bike riding teens: protective clothing.
And there’s a company in this space whose gear I’ve become a big fan of:
Beyond Riders
I’ve tested a number of their products
over the last couple of years
, and what I like most is that they don’t look like motorcycle gear, even though they offer much of the same protection.
Their hoodies, riding shirts, jeans, and jackets can be fitted with CE-rated Level 1 or even Level 2 armor at the shoulders, elbows, and back, giving riders meaningful impact protection without making them look like they’re headed to a racetrack.
And let me be clear from the start: I don’t get any kickbacks for this, no affiliate links, nothing. I just really like their gear, and I support what they’re doing: making safe riding clothes that look good and don’t give the impression that I’m heading off to the closest biker bar.
Believe it or not, this hoodie has motorcycle armor in the chest, back, elbows, and shoulders, plus is built for the slide!
My personal favorite is the armored hoodie, above. It looks just like the kind of hoodie most teenagers already wear every day, which means they’re actually more likely to keep it on instead of leaving it at home.
The fit is comfortable, the styling is casual, and the built-in armor disappears into the garment. You wouldn’t know it, but behind the abrasion-resistant textiles are CE Level 2 armor in the shoulders, elbows, back, and chest.
There are even hidden features, like secret pockets and a hidden microfiber cloth in the corner for quickly cleaning your sunglasses.
The riding shirt feels like a light canvas jacket but packs in motorcycle-level protection
I’m also a big fan of Beyond Riders’ canvas riding jacket. It looks like a canvas overshirt or lightweight jacket, but underneath that casual appearance is full armor in the shoulders, back, and elbows, along with abrasion-resistant materials designed to help prevent painful road rash if you end up sliding across pavement.
In fact, Beyond Riders has become popular not just with e-bike riders, but also with electric skateboard riders and even motorcyclists who want protective gear that doesn’t scream “motorcycle.”
No piece of gear can eliminate the risk of a crash, but quality protective clothing can absolutely reduce the consequences. As more teenagers discover the freedom and independence that e-bikes provide, it’s worth thinking beyond just the bike itself. Pair that new e-bike with a quality helmet and some protective riding apparel, and you’ll be giving your young rider a much better chance of walking away from the unexpected.

content:

Is Volvo launching an electric sedan?
After pulling the S90 and V60 Cross Country, Volvo will no longer offer sedans or wagons in the US, leaving its lineup consisting of just SUVs and crossovers.
The Swedish automaker is revamping its lineup as it navigates the Trump Administration’s policy changes.
Importing vehicles from Europe has become too costly, and Volvo has struggled to sell electric vehicles following the elimination of the federal EV tax credit last September.
For that reason, Volvo is
discontinuing the EX30
in the US after the 2026 model year, its smallest electric SUV.
The Single Motor EX30 variant was expected to go on sale as one of the most affordable EVs in the US, starting at around $ 35,000, but Volvo dropped the electric SUV from its lineup altogether, citing “market conditions and financial factors.”
According to
Automotive News
, Volvo is eyeing a return to the small-car market with a midsize electric sedan and wagon.
Volvo would build the two new vehicles in Europe, while both would be underpinned by its new SPA3 platform.
While the new EVs are expected to arrive in the second half of 2028, another new Volvo sedan was captured for the first time.
The images posted on
NewCarScoops
show the vehicle heavily camouflaged. Despite the disguise, you can see it’s equipped with a roof-mounted LiDAR, but it still has exhaust pipes underneath, suggesting it will use a gas engine.
Keep in mind this is still an early-stage test vehicle, and the actual production model could change.
Volvo is also expected to launch a new plug-in hybrid (PHEV) and traditional hybrid options, including updated versions of the XC40, XC60, and XC90, so a refreshed S70 hybrid could be in the works.
While Volvo is introducing new hybrid and plug-in hybrid models, it isn’t abandoning pure electric vehicles altogether.
The 2027 EX60 is
now on sale
, starting at $58,400. As the first vehicle based on its SPA3 platform, the electric SUV is Volvo’s longest-range, fast-charging, and most technologically advanced EV to date.
Volvo said the range-topping EX60 P12 AWD will go on sale later this year, offering an estimated range of up to 400 miles. The P10 grade, currently on sale, offers an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 330 miles. It can also add up to 165 miles in 10 minutes of charging.

The aging EX40 is expected to be replaced by

title: Archer makes wild deal with Boeing swapping eVTOL startups for equity
content:
Archer Aviation
Fred Lambert
| Aug 10 2026 - 7:35 am PT
Archer Aviation is buying three of Boeing’s aerospace subsidiaries: autonomous air-taxi developer Wisk Aero, military drone maker Insitu, and airspace-software firm SkyGrid. The deal also hands Boeing a stake in Archer.
Investors loved it. Archer (ACHR) stock jumped more than 20% on Monday, and the acquisition instantly turns a pre-revenue eVTOL startup into a company with a profitable defense business behind it.
It could accelerate Archer’s eVTOL plans.
What Archer is buying
Insitu is the prize. It’s a defense drone maker generating over $200 million in annual revenue, it’s profitable, and it has built more than 3,500 uncrewed aircraft systems fielded by the armed forces of 35 nations.
Wisk Aero is the autonomous eVTOL developer Boeing has bankrolled for years. Archer says it’s the only company to design, build, and fly six generations of eVTOL aircraft, with more than 1,700 flight tests. SkyGrid rounds out the deal with aircraft-agnostic air traffic management software.
Financial terms weren’t disclosed. Boeing isn’t only selling here. It’s taking a stake in Archer and entering a technology-sharing collaboration, though no purchase price, investment amount, or equity percentage was announced. The deal is expected to close by the end of 2026, pending antitrust review.
The “physical AI” pitch
Archer is selling this as a bet on “physical AI.” The company says combining autonomy, eVTOL aircraft, and drones creates “an end-to-end physical AI platform for aerospace and defense,” all feeding into Archer’s own AI foundation model, ZEE.
“This is a watershed moment for Archer and the future of physical AI in aerospace and defense,” said founder and CEO Adam Goldstein. “This is the next big step forward in becoming a diversified platform.”
Boeing kept its framing simpler. “This transaction is a win-win for Boeing and Archer,” said Brian Yutko, Boeing’s VP of Commercial Airplanes Product Development. “It allows Wisk, SkyGrid and Insitu to accelerate capability development and time to market.”
The move accelerates a defense pivot Archer started in late 2024, when it partnered with Anduril to build a hybrid VTOL military aircraft and raised $430 million. Last month, the two unveiled Thunder, a jointly developed autonomous VTOL aircraft for defense and commercial missions. Insitu gives that ambition real revenue and real contracts instead of renderings.
Archer’s core business keeps moving in the meantime. It
began piloted operations of its flagship Midnight aircraft
last year, and it’s the
exclusive air taxi provider for the 2028 LA Olympics
The rivals who used to sue each other
There’s history here. Wisk sued Archer in 2021, accusing it of stealing trade secrets, in a bitter multi-year court fight. The two settled on August 10, 2023, with Boeing investing in
Archer’s funding round
and the companies agreeing to collaborate on autonomy.
That settlement was exactly three years ago today. Now Archer owns Wisk outright.
Electrek’s Take
The “physical AI” branding is doing a lot of work. Every startup slaps AI on a press release now, and Archer is no exception. But strip the buzzword and the logic holds up. Archer just bought its way from pre-revenue promise to a real defense business with $200 million in revenue and drones flying in 35 countries.
For a company that has burned cash for years chasing FAA certification, buying Insitu’s profitable, cash-generating business changes the entire company overnight. It steadies the balance sheet with real manufacturing and contracts, which until now were mostly a splashy unveiling and a stock pop.
I think there’s a real chance that it will accelerate the advent of eVTOLs, but I remain skeptical. I would keep a close eye on Archer becoming more focused on its new defense business, which I don’t really care for, at the detriment of its promise of commercial electric flight.

title: Musk's Terafab chip plant will run on gas, not Tesla solar
content:
Fred Lambert
| Aug 10 2026 - 6:55 am PT
SpaceX confirmed it will power Terafab, its $16.8 billion chip megafactory in Texas, with its own natural gas power plants and “very large battery arrays.” Tesla solar isn’t in the plan.
That’s despite Tesla being a partner on the project, and despite Tesla selling solar panels, Powerwalls, and grid-scale batteries built for exactly this kind of load.
A chip fab on the bones of a coal plant
Tesla and SpaceX
confirmed Terafab last week
: a semiconductor plant in Grimes County, Texas, about an hour northwest of Houston, that the companies call the largest chip manufacturing facility on the planet. The first phase runs $16.8 billion, down from a $25 billion figure floated in March. It’s meant to churn out over a terawatt of compute per year for SpaceX and xAI data centers, plus future chips for Tesla’s Optimus and Cybercab.
Here’s the detail that got buried. The plant sits on the site of a former coal-fired power plant, and SpaceX plans to power it with newly built natural gas plants and batteries. So the compute future gets built on the same fossil ground as the past. Just swap coal for gas.
There’s no mention of Tesla solar anywhere in the power plan, even though Tesla co-owns the project.
The same gas playbook, only bigger
None of this is a one-off. It’s the pattern.
xAI’s Colossus data center around Memphis has been running on gas turbines since 2024, many of them unpermitted. The NAACP, the Southern Environmental Law Center, and Earthjustice are suing over 27 unpermitted turbines in Southaven, Mississippi, that they say pump out more than 1,700 tons of nitrogen oxides and 19 tons of formaldehyde a year next to homes, schools, and churches. “A data center should not be a potential death sentence for a community’s health,” said the NAACP’s Abre’ Conner. When regulators moved in,
Trump’s DOJ intervened to keep the turbines running
on national-security grounds.
Then Musk
personally bought gas turbine company APR Energy for about $1 billion
in July, picking up more than a gigawatt of turbine capacity. SpaceX has separately committed more than $2.8 billion to gas turbines to power its data centers. Terafab’s on-site gas plants are the next brick in that wall.
Tesla sells the alternative — Musk just won’t buy it
The strange part is that the cleaner option lives inside Musk’s own companies.
Tesla sells solar, Powerwall, and Megapack. xAI itself bought $269 million of Tesla Megapacks earlier this year. In June, Tesla and Sunrun
launched a 16 GW virtual power plant pitched directly at data centers
. Tesla is literally marketing solar-plus-storage as an answer to AI power demand.
And this is the same Musk who spent years selling a “solar electric economy,” who once
pitched space-based solar as the long-term fix
while burning gas on the ground. The vision is solar. The buildout is gas.
Electrek’s Take
Running gigawatt-scale, 24/7 chip fabs and AI training clusters on solar alone is genuinely difficult today. You need firm power, but Tesla’s and solar plus battery expertise is the solution.
But that’s not the choice Musk is making. He’s not building a solar-and-gas hybrid and squeezing the gas down over time. He’s going gas-first with zero Tesla solar. The driver here isn’t physics, it’s speed and cost.
It’s also incentives. Yes, this would be a great project for Tesla, which Musk owns about 20% of, but it is an even better project for Musk’s newly acquired APR Energy, which he owns 100% of.
Tesla used to exist to accelerate the transition to sustainable energy. Its founder is now behind one of the biggest new gas buildouts in the country.

title: BYD's kei EV already looks like a hit with over 1,000 orders in its first 2 weeks
content:
BYD’s first electric kei car received over 1,000 orders in just two weeks after it went on sale.
BYD Racco EV orders reach over 1,000 in two weeks
BYD is going where no foreign brand has gone before. The Chinese EV giant officially launched Racco on July 28, its first electric kei vehicle, specifically designed to crack open Japan’s tiny-car market, long dominated by domestic brands like Nissan, Honda, Toyota, and Suzuki.
The Racco is already off to a promising start. BYD announced on Monday that its new mini EV received over 1,000 cumulative orders in its first two weeks on the market.
BYD said it was “the fastest pace for any model introduced to date,” and the vehicle was “attracting significant attention throughout Japan.”
According to a survey from early buyers, the Racco is exceeding expectations for its “excellent cost-performance ratio,” features, and craftsmanship.
About 80% of buyers chose the more expensive Racco 300 Premium trim, 14% chose the Plus, and the remaining 6% chose the base 200 model.
Interestingly, 37.5% of buyers added the Racco as an additional vehicle, 35.7% replaced their old vehicle, and 26.8% purchased it as a new vehicle.
BYD said 55.4% of early buyers already had EV charging equipment at home, 43% did not, and 1.6% did not answer.
Why are buyers interested? For one, BYD’s electric kei car is more efficient and, thanks to its electric powertrain, it also has lower maintenance costs. The Racco offers more advanced features as a software-defined vehicle (SDV), and with software updates it will continue to introduce new features, much like a smartphone.
BYD’s electric kei car starts at just ¥2,145,000, or about $13,000 in Japan. The base Racco 200 uses a 22.4 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery with a WLTC driving range of 210 km (130 miles).
The higher-priced 300 Plus and Premium trims use a larger 35.84 kWh battery with a range up to 320 km (199 miles), which BYD said makes it the first kei EV in Japan to offer over 300 km.

Top comment by jrharbort
BYD will do well in Japan where others have failed due to two big reasons. 1) They understand the market and its needs. Inflation has spiraled out of control even in Japan while wages have hardly gone up. An extremely affordable and highly capable electric KEI car for those that need a car will be very attractive because 2) Japan imports all of their oil and are extremely sensitive to price fluctuations caused by conflicts. These cars will help to weaken that reliance on energy imports.
While Honda’s N-Box, Japan’s best-selling vehicle, is slightly cheaper, starting at ¥1,739,100 ($10,500), BYD’s kei EV is eligible for a ¥150,000 ($900) government subsidy, bringing the Racco’s starting price to ¥1,995,000 ($12,200).
The Racco is cheaper than the Nissan Sakura, Japan’s current best-selling EV, which starts at ¥2,448,600 ($15,000) and offers a longer driving range. It’s no wonder buyers are lining up for it.

title: Why does Monarc build its e-bikes with their forks on backward?
content:
Micah Toll
| Aug 10 2026 - 5:37 am PT
If you’ve spotted one of Monarc’s new e-bikes, there’s a good chance one of your first thoughts was,
“Wait… did they install the fork backwards?”
The answer is no, it’s not really on backward – despite how it may look. Monarc just uses what’s known as a reverse-arch suspension fork, a design that’s uncommon in the cycling world but one that offers several engineering advantages.
Instead of placing the fork brace in front of the fork wheel like most suspension forks, Monarc’s in-house designed Gneiss fork moves that arch to the rear, allowing it to be shorter and stiffer.
It’s an eye-catcher on the company’s flagship
Monarc Marker off-road e-bike
, but it has a very specific purpose.
While it might look unusual, the concept isn’t new. Reverse-arch forks have appeared before in mountain biking and motorcycle suspension, where engineers have long appreciated the potential benefits.
They were originally patented by Manitou, appearing for years on those high-end mountain bikes.
But when the patent expired a few years ago, others were able to incorporate the design. Monarc is the latest yet,
bringing a more refined and better-performing fork design to e-bikes
in a way that has never been this accessible.
According to Monarc, relocating the arch allows the fork to be lighter while also increasing stiffness and strength.
Greater fore-aft rigidity can help the front wheel track more precisely through rough terrain, improving steering accuracy and reducing unwanted flex under braking or hard impacts. The company says it achieved those gains while still providing 80 mm of suspension travel for trail riding.
There’s also a practical advantage. By moving the arch rearward, mud, sticks, and trail debris have less opportunity to become trapped between the tire and fork brace. It’s a small detail, but one off-road riders will appreciate.
It’s a rarity in the e-bike industry, but refreshing to see companies experimenting with genuine engineering rather than simply changing colors or frame shapes. Monarc says it developed the Gneiss fork entirely in-house, giving its engineers the freedom to rethink one of the most recognizable components on an e-bike.
So no, Monarc didn’t accidentally install the forks backward. They just chose a different solution to the same engineering challenge – and one that happens to turn a few heads along the way.

title: Bangladesh reinstates payment guarantees to attract renewable energy investment - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Bangladesh has reinstated payment guarantees for renewable energy projects to boost investor confidence and attract local and international financing. Industry stakeholders say the move could improve project bankability, unlock new solar projects and help ease the country’s ongoing power crisis.
Syful Islam
10 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Utility-scale
Image: Fredrik Rubensson, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0
The government of Bangladesh has restored the provision of payment guarantees for renewable energy projects to attract new investment amid a severe energy crisis. The provision was reinstated following repeated requests from industry stakeholders, two years after it was scrapped by the previous government.
The absence of a government payment guarantee had deterred local and foreign investors from making new investments, amid uncertainty over payments for electricity supplied to the grid.
The Power Division signs payment guarantees with independent power producers (IPPs) on behalf of the government, while the Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB) signs power purchase agreements with them. A payment guarantee from the Power Division helps IPPs secure financing from local and international banks to develop power plants.
The Power Division recently instructed the BPDB to include payment guarantees in future tender documents. The directive was issued in a letter signed by Muhammad Abul Lyse, deputy secretary of the Power Division.
“With the objective of increasing electricity generation from renewable energy sources, instructions are hereby issued to invite tenders by including the provision of Payment Guarantee under the power purchase agreement and implementation agreement,” the directive states.
Industry stakeholders have welcomed the move, saying the restoration of payment guarantees will provide greater security for investors and help renewable energy developers secure financing from local and international lenders.
Ezaz Al Qudrat A Mazid, managing director of Solar EPC Development Ltd, said the initiative would improve project bankability, strengthen lender confidence and make it easier to attract both local and international investment to the sector.
“It is a positive signal for developers, financiers, and technology partners committed to Bangladesh’s clean energy transition,” he said, adding that the initiative would help unlock new renewable energy projects and support the country’s long-term sustainable energy goals.
Mostafa Al Mahmud, president of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association (BSREA), said that if the previous government had not canceled the payment guarantee provision, several solar power plants could have come online over the past two years.
“That could have helped lessen the ongoing power crisis, which led to factory shutdowns, job losses, increased power cuts, and immense suffering among people,” he told
pv magazine
Mahmud also called for the immediate removal of duties on all solar power equipment, including battery energy storage systems, as well as incentives to encourage the use of solar power.

title: When the rivers stop flowing: Europe’s drought summer measured - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
River-flow, generation and price data from April to July 2026 point to a drought corridor stretching from the Rhine delta to the lower Danube. Hydropower output across the corridor was about one-fifth below the recent norm, falling by a third to a half in the worst-hit systems. Nuclear plants along the Danube also cut output as river flows dropped to their lowest levels in seven years. Gas, imports and unusually wet conditions in Iberia helped offset the shortfall, but at steadily rising prices.
10 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Extreme historical low water level of the Rhine in August 2026 | Image: Rolf Kranz, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
The hydrology deteriorated in slow motion. Modelled daily discharge, the volume of water flowing past a fixed point, for the Rhine at Lobith, where the river enters the Netherlands, averaged 81% of its 2019 to 25 norm in April, 66% in May, 58% in June and 37% in July. Twenty-seven days in 2026 fell below the lowest single day recorded at that station in the previous seven Aprils to Julys, a period that includes the drought of 2022. The July figure deserves a second look: the 2026 monthly average of 850 m3/s sits below the lowest single July day of the entire 2019 to 25 baseline, 880 m3/s, recorded in the drought summer of 2022. An average month in 2026 was worse than the worst day of the previous seven years.
Modelled daily Rhine discharge at Lobith, 2026 against the 2019-25 monthly mean and the lowest single day of that period. Image: Copernicus GloFAS via Open-Meteo
France ran dry from the south. The Garonne at Tonneins averaged 5% of its normal July flow, with sixteen days below anything seen in 2019 to 25. The Loire at Saumur reached 13% of normal in July and the Rhone at Beaucaire 41%. On the Danube the squeeze built downstream: flow through the Iron Gates, the river’s largest hydro complex, ran at 58% of normal in May, 54% in June and 48% in July, and five July days ran below anything in the station’s 2019 to 25 record.
Monthly river flow as a share of the 2019-25 average at nine stations, with the count of 2026 days below any single day of the baseline period. Image: Copernicus GloFAS via Open-Meteo
Hydro: losses in the drought corridor, gains in Iberia
Generation patterns closely tracked river conditions. The seven corridor systems, Austria, Italy, Romania, Serbia, Hungary, Slovakia and France taken together, produced roughly 13 TWh less hydro between April and July than the 2019 to 25 average for the same months, a shortfall of one fifth. Austria was down 34% in July, Italy 38%, Serbia 34%, Romania 32% and Hungary 53%. France flipped from a wet spring, 6% to 7% above normal in April and May, to 16% and 17% below in June and July. The correlation data confirms how direct the link is: daily Serbian run-of-river output, from plants that generate directly on the current without a storage dam, tracked Iron Gates flow with a correlation of 0.89, and French run-of-river tracked the Rhone at 0.73. Run-of-river generation moved closely with changing river conditions.
Several neighboring systems experienced considerably stronger hydrological conditions. Portuguese hydro ran 117% above its norm in July after a rain-heavy first half, Spain finished the window 16% to 44% above normal by month, and Swiss output opened 64% above norm in April on strong melt before converging to 5% above by July as the snow reserve ran out. Together the wet flanks added roughly 9 TWh against the baseline, offsetting about 70% of the corridor’s loss at continental level, but not in the places that needed it. Reservoir data sharpens the picture for the autumn: by mid-July, Italian and Romanian storage stood closer to the 2015 to 25 minimum than to the median, Spanish reservoirs sat near the top of their historical band, and Portuguese storage held above its median.
Monthly hydro generation, 2026 against the 2019-25 average for the same month. Image: ENTSO-E Transparency Platform
Nuclear on a warm, shallow river
The Danube plants illustrate the most acute impacts observed in late July. At Cernavoda in Romania, both units were offline on nineteen May days during the spring outage season. One unit carried June alone at around 15 GWh per day, the second returned in early July and lifted output to around 26, and over the final three days of the month output fell back to 15 GWh per day against a July norm near 29, at the bottom of a month in which Danube flow through the Iron Gates averaged 48% of normal. In Hungary, Paks fell from 38 GWh per day on July 28 to 21 on July 31, a cut of 45% in three days and its lowest level of the entire window. Bulgarian nuclear output had already run 22% below its June norm. The instructive detail sits in the temperature series: riverside air at Paks exceeded 32 C on only six July days. The observed output reductions coincided more closely with river conditions than with periods of extreme air temperature.
Daily nuclear generation in Hungary and Romania with riverside air temperature at the plant sites, April to July 2026. Image: ENTSO-E, Open-Meteo
France showed the other face of the same exposure, and the national data keeps the two forces in proportion. Riverside air at the Golfech site on the Garonne reached 35 C or more on ten July days, and the Garonne itself carried 5% of its normal July flow. Yet French fleet output ran 10% to 15% above its 2019 to 25 norm in every month of the window, and the summer’s lowest single days, 792 GWh in late June and 831 GWh on July 12, remained shallow against a fleet averaging roughly 945 GWh per day. Whatever heat management individual river-cooled units required, it stayed episodic and site-specific in the aggregate series. The Danube plants showed a markedly different pattern from that observed in France: river conditions that coincided with substantial output reductions. Switzerland sat in between. National nuclear output ran 12% to 23% below norm in April and May, a period in which the public series cannot separate maintenance schedules from river conditions, and daily output fell 16% over the final four days of July.
Coal, barges and the Rhine question
Low water on the Rhine constrains barge loading and raises fuel logistics costs on the corridor before it removes megawatt-hours. In the generation data, German coal output showed no clean flow signal: its correlation with Kaub discharge across the window was 0.20, and monthly coal output moved with wind conditions rather than with the river. The pattern is consistent with plants drawing on fuel stocks and rail alternatives, so that the constraint surfaced first as cost rather than as lost output. Serbia was the exception in the coal data, cutting lignite-fired generation by roughly 0.7 TWh against 2025 while raising imports, concentrated in the hottest weeks of the window.
How systems compensated for reduced hydro output, and at what price
Each system balanced the shortfall differently. Italy replaced 3.6 TWh of lost hydro, measured against 2025, with 4.1 TWh of additional gas-fired generation, plus 1.1 TWh of new solar. Austria covered a 2.4 TWh hydro shortfall mainly with electricity imports, measured here as the gap between national consumption and generation and 1.6 TWh higher than a year earlier, and 0.9 TWh of added solar. Switzerland combined 1.4 TWh of additional net imports with nuclear output 0.5 TWh higher than a year earlier. Serbia substituted imports for both water and coal. Romania experienced one of the more constrained adjustment paths: national consumption ran roughly 1.2 TWh below 2025 across the window, in a period of surging regional prices and constrained domestic units. Solar provided positive year-on-year generation growth across all reporting corridor markets, adding output year on year in every corridor market that reports it to ENTSO-E, from 0.3 TWh in Hungary to 0.9 TWh in Austria and 1.1 TWh in Italy, alongside 5.4 TWh in Spain.
Change in April-July generation and net position against 2025, by fuel. Net imports are proxied by load minus generation. Image: ENTSO-E Transparency Platform
Nuclear and hydro are among the technologies that power systems typically rely on for sustained output. This summer, both showed varying degrees of exposure to water availability in several drought-affected regions. Strong production in a normal year does not necessarily indicate how a system will perform during periods of extreme water stress. Along drought-affected sections of the corridor, hydro losses coincided with reductions at selected river-cooled nuclear stations. The observed response relied on imports, additional gas-fired generation and solar output, which together offset part of the shortfall.
Interconnection moved Alpine and Balkan deficits to better-supplied neighbors, gas-fired generation increased significantly in Italy, and solar added output across the corridor, the one major generation source in this analysis whose output was not directly constrained by river availability. No single technology offset the loss alone, but the combination of generation sources and cross-border imports absorbed simultaneous reductions in hydro output and output constraints at selected river-cooled nuclear stations.
The market impact of replacing lost hydro generation intensified through the summer. In the day-ahead market, the wholesale reference price set one day before delivery, July averages reached €122 ($140.9)/MWh in Hungary against €103 a year earlier, €120 in Romania, €117 in Austria against €88, and €117 in Switzerland against €91. France averaged €95/MWh against €58 in July 2025. The daily pattern shows two distinct shocks: a heat-demand spike that pushed Hungarian, Romanian and Serbian daily averages above €225/MWh on July 1, and then a grinding climb through late July as rivers emptied, with Swiss daily prices averaging €134/MWh over July 22 to 31. The price impact associated with drought conditions appeared persistent rather than short-lived, because recovery in river conditions typically occurs more slowly than short-lived weather events.
Monthly and daily day-ahead prices, April to July, 2026 against 2025. Image: ENTSO-E Transparency Platform
How WSP’s Electricity Market Outlook can help
Do you need to know how a hydro portfolio, a river-cooled plant or a cross-border position performs in a repeat of this summer, or in a drier one? These are the types of questions assessed using WSP’s Electricity Market Outlook (EMO). The underlying model, PRIMES-IEM, sits behind two decades of European Commission policy analysis. It runs all European markets simultaneously to 2050, with cross-border flows derived by replicating the EUPHEMIA algorithm used by ENTSO-E. Outputs cover hourly prices, capture rates, hydro and cooling-water sensitivity scenarios, curtailment exposure and BESS profitability projections at country and asset level, the quantitative inputs commonly used in PPA structuring, adequacy assessment and project-finance analysis.

title: Clemson University designs solar-integrated electric vehicle - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The Deep Orange 17 is an electric vehicle prototype designed to generate more energy than it consumes during a typical day of urban commuting.
Patrick Jowett
10 Aug 2026
Research & Development
Technology & Products
Image: Clemson University
Students at Clemson University in the US state of South Carolina have developed a solar-integrated electric vehicle.
Known as Deep Orange 17, the vehicle is designed to generate more energy than it consumes during a typical day of urban commuting.
The vehicle features a solar energy system which, according to a statement published by the university, forms a core part of the vehicle’s propulsion strategy rather than serving as an auxiliary feature.
The solar PV system features more than 1,700 solar cells which are integrated into the vehicle’s exterior surfaces, meaning it harvests energy while both parked and in motion. The PV system is protected by a durable outer film.
“The system continuously replenishes the vehicle’s energy storage using sunlight, helping offset energy consumed during daily driving,” the university’s statement explains.
The vehicle’s structure also features structural steel with aluminum components, carbon fiber structural members and 3D-printed metal joints. It weighs in at approximately 550 kg, making it approximately one-fourth the weight of many similarly-sized production vehicles.
Additional technologies include regenerative braking, intelligent torque distribution and optimized drivetrain controls, which the university says work together to maximize energy recovery and improve overall vehicle performance.
To assess real-world performance, students modeled environmental conditions and solar availability in Greenville, South Carolina, as well as in the German city of Frankfurt, Spanish capital Madrid and Mumbai in India. They found the vehicle capable of producing enough excess solar energy to add an average 50 km of driving range during a daily 20 km commute across each of the locations.
Harsh Manghnani, Deep Orange team member and solar integration lead, said that seeing the initial research and design validated in a working prototype has been “incredibly rewarding.”
“This was an incredibly challenging project – not only to create a working energy-positive prototype, but to demonstrate how a vehicle can become increasingly energy independent through solar integration,” Manghnani said.
Deep Orange 17 was developed in collaboration with BMW’s research and development team, with researchers from Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE helping with the solar PV system.
Research on the prototype is set to continue at Clemson University’s International Center for Automotive Research, while the vehicle itself is scheduled to feature at the 2027 Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas.

title: Advanced sodium-ion battery prototypes now approaching 200 Wh/kg - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
An international team of scientists has reviewed recent advances in sodium-ion battery components, highlighting their potential as a lower-cost, more sustainable alternative to lithium-ion batteries. The researchers identify key challenges including lower energy density, shorter cycle life and manufacturing constraints, while pointing to advances in materials and electrolytes as important to future commercialization.
Lior Kahana
10 Aug 2026
Research & Development
Batteries
Energy Storage
A sodium-ion battery cell developed by Hithium
An international team of scientists has conducted a literature review of recent advances and future prospects for key components of sodium-ion batteries (SIBs).
SIBs store and release energy by shuttling sodium ions between the cathode and anode through an electrolyte during charging and discharging. They are considered an attractive alternative to lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) because sodium is abundant and more evenly distributed geographically.
“The growing need for affordable and sustainable energy storage solutions across important end-use sectors, including automotive, industrial and energy storage, is contributing to the robust expansion of the global sodium-ion battery market,” corresponding author Ababay Ketema Worku told
pv magazine
“SIBs are still in their early stages, even though first-generation commercial devices from companies such as Contemporary Amperex Technology, Faradion and TIAMAT have already entered the energy storage market, targeting light-mobility and stationary applications,” he added. “Despite their long-term performance, economic and environmental benefits, SIB penetration remains low worldwide, and the market is expected to grow significantly over the next 10 years.”
Among the factors limiting wider SIB adoption, Worku cited lower energy density and shorter cycle life compared with LIBs. These limitations are largely linked to sodium’s larger ionic radius, which places greater mechanical stress on electrode materials and can accelerate degradation.
Other challenges include higher self-discharge rates, underdeveloped supply chains for battery-grade materials, and inefficiencies in manufacturing processes, including slurry formulation, electrode drying and cell assembly.
“Although SIBs have better thermal stability and are compatible with existing LIB infrastructure, sophisticated management systems and predictive modeling methods, such as computational fluid dynamics, differential scanning calorimetry and thermogravimetric analysis, are needed to ensure pack-level safety,” Worku said.
The review examines five major classes of SIB anodes: alloy-based, intercalation-based, conversion-based, organic and MXene-based materials. The researchers found that carbon-based, alloy and organic anodes offer strong cycling stability and sodium-storage capacity, while conversion-type materials provide high theoretical capacities.
However, widespread adoption of these materials remains constrained by issues including large volume changes during cycling, poor electrical conductivity, unstable interfaces and structural degradation. These challenges are driving continued research into advanced material designs and nanostructuring.
The researchers concluded that future progress will depend on the development of more stable cathode and anode materials, safer and more conductive electrolytes, and separators with improved thermal and chemical stability. They also emphasized that advances across all battery components, including electrodes, electrolytes, binders, current collectors, conductive additives and solvents, will be essential to accelerate commercialization and make SIBs more competitive with LIBs.
“Currently, the energy densities of SIBs range from 100 Wh/kg to 160 Wh/kg, with some advanced prototypes approaching 200 Wh/kg,” Worku said. “Improved electrolyte formulations that boost ionic conductivity and electrochemical stability, as well as developments in electrode materials, are primarily responsible for these advances.”
Worku said energy storage is one of several areas in which SIBs are finding new applications.
“They are ideal for load balancing applications, electric vehicles (EVs), renewable energy integration and large-scale energy storage, due to their low cost and utilization of readily available raw materials,” he said. “SIBs offer a scalable and affordable alternative for storing and delivering renewable energy, and pilot projects have demonstrated their promise for grid stability. Sodium-ion batteries are becoming more popular in the automotive industry as a more cost-effective substitute for lithium-ion batteries, especially for electric two- and three-wheelers.”
The review was presented “
Recent advances and future perspectives on key components for sodium-ion batteries
” has appeared in
Energy Conversion and Management: X
. Scientists from the
University of South Africa
, Ethiopia’s
Bahir Dar University
, and China’s
Shanghai University
have conducted the study.

title: Italy to allocate 10 GW of PV under new FerX incentive scheme - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The Italian government has finalized the FerX mechanism, setting a 10 GW quota for PV projects and a reference strike price of €80/MWh, with premiums for floating and asbestos-roof replacement projects.
Massimiliano Tripodo
10 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Image: Capcora
Italy’s Ministry of Environment and Energy Security (MASE) has published Decree 194/2026, setting out the final version of the FerX mechanism. The measure, which follows the EU’s approval of the mechanism in June, entered into force on Aug. 7 and applies to solar, wind and hydropower plants, as well as facilities for treating residual gases.
For photovoltaic plants, the decree establishes a 10 GW capacity quota. The reference strike price is set at €80 ($92.4)/MWh. The decree provides two flexibility thresholds for plants participating in competitive bidding: the price may rise to €95/MWh (upper strike price) under particularly high-cost conditions, or fall to €65/MWh (lower strike price) under particularly low-cost conditions.
Two additional premiums are available: €27/MWh for photovoltaic systems installed to replace Eternit or asbestos roofing, and €10/MWh for systems installed on bodies of water.
A safeguard clause limits simplified access for small-scale systems. The mechanism for plants with a capacity of up to 1 MW will cease to apply on Dec. 31, 2030, or 60 days after the 10 GW capacity quota is reached, whichever comes first.
Plants of up to 1 MW that begin construction after the decree enters into force will have direct access to the support mechanism without having to participate in competitive bidding. For this capacity segment, the Regulatory Authority for Energy, Networks and Environment (ARERA) must define the award prices within 90 days of the decree entering into force.
For plants larger than 1 MW, participation in competitive procedures is mandatory. The mechanism is not available to projects for which construction work began before the application was submitted.
For plants larger than 10 MW subject to a single authorization (AU), the decree introduces an expedited project assessment procedure. Within 30 days of the authorization being issued, Italian energy agency Gestore dei servizi energetici (GSE) must issue an opinion to the project proponent confirming whether the project is eligible to apply for the mechanism.
The decree requires MASE, based on data provided by Terna and the GSE, to periodically update the quotas and coefficients specified in the tender notices, at least once every two years.
PV plants that secure a successful ranking must enter into operation within 36 months. The decree specifies that this deadline excludes any periods of downtime caused by
force majeure
during construction of the plant and its associated infrastructure.
In the event of a delay, the awarded price will be reduced by 0.2% per month for the first nine months and by 0.5% per month for the following six months, for a maximum total delay of 15 months. If the delay exceeds this limit, the GSE will revoke the plant’s ranking and call in the final performance bond. If the plant is subsequently admitted to a support mechanism, the awarded price will be reduced by a further 5%.
Within 60 days of the decree entering into force, MASE must approve, based on a proposal from the GSE, the operational rules for accessing the mechanism. Within the following 30 days, the GSE must publish the public notice for the submission of preliminary qualification applications.
The decree also allows plants located in neighboring countries to participate, provided an agreement is in place between the relevant country and Italy.
Access to the FerX mechanism may be combined exclusively with one of the following measures: capital grants of up to 40% of the investment cost for newly constructed plants; guarantee and revolving funds; or tax incentives in the form of tax credits or deductions from business income for investments in machinery and equipment.

title: Zinc oxide UV shield cuts heterojunction solar cell degradation and boosts lifetime output by 4.8% - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers in China have demonstrated that zinc oxide (ZnO) thin films can act as a ‘sunscreen’ for heterojunction solar cells, reducing UV-induced degradation while maintaining high visible-light transmission. ZnO-coated modules achieved lower projected LCOE and 4.8% higher cumulative power generation over 25 years.
Emiliano Bellini
10 Aug 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Image: Southwest Petroleum University
Researchers at the
Southwest Petroleum University
in China have tested zinc oxide (ZnO) thin films to protect silicon heterojunction (HJT) solar cells from UV-induced degradation (UV-ID) and have found that they can increase cumulative power output by 4.8%
“Current approaches to mitigating UV-ID can be broadly divided into two categories. At the material level, encapsulation materials are primarily used to achieve UV cutoff or UV conversion, thereby blocking or converting incident high-energy UV photons. At the device level, structural optimization is employed to enhance UV resistance, although its potential for further improvement is relatively limited,” the research’s corresponding author, Jian Yu, told
pv magazine
“We proposed a protection strategy based on wide-bandgap metal oxides, using ZnO as a representative example. By efficiently absorbing and blocking high-energy UV photons, a physical protective barrier analogous to a ‘sunscreen’ is formed on the cell surface, effectively suppressing UV-ID from a materials perspective,” he went on to say. “Although the ZnO film may temporarily affect the electrical performance of the cell, a comprehensive assessment from the perspective of long-term reliability over the full photovoltaic module lifecycle shows that the resulting UV resistance gain and extended service life can achieve superior overall cost-effectiveness.”
The researchers explained that ZnO is a promising UV-shielding material for solar cells because of its wide bandgap. It can absorb UV photons in the 300–400 nm range, complementing the spectral response of crystalline silicon. This complementary absorption can reduce short-wavelength photon losses while improving the theoretical photovoltaic potential of silicon devices.
The scientists investigated protection strategies: direct deposition of ZnO onto the TCO surface of pre-metallized HJT cells and deposition onto the front glass of finished modules. The ZnO films were prepared by DC magnetron sputtering, with their optical properties controlled through deposition power, pressure, oxygen flow, and substrate temperature.
The films were found to exhibit only about 16–18% transmittance in the UV region while maintaining an average visible transmittance above 90%. They also effectively functioned as a UV-cutoff layer without significantly compromising visible-light transmission, as they absorbed high-energy UV photons before they reach the underlying HJT structure, thereby reducing UV-induced damage.
The research group also ascertained that direct deposition of ZnO on the cells reduced minority-carrier lifetime degradation from 54.9% to 32.6% after exposure to 60 kWh/m² of UV radiation. Although ZnO initially caused a slight performance loss due to parasitic absorption in the visible spectrum, it significantly mitigated long-term UV-induced degradation. After the same UV dose, power conversion efficiency degradation was limited to 3.49%, compared with 5.74% for uncoated cells.
ZnO-coated glass was found to provide even stronger protection, with full-area coverage limiting carrier-lifetime degradation to 24.9% after 40 kWh/m² of UV exposure. After 60 kWh/m², ZnO-covered cells recorded short-circuit current and efficiency degradation of just 1.23% and 2.31%, respectively, compared with 2.75% and 4.72% for cells without ZnO.
Module-level tests further showed that ZnO-coated glass reduced efficiency degradation from 4.99% to 4.12% after 60 kWh/m² of UV exposure. Over a projected 25-year operating period, ZnO-protected modules were estimated to achieve a lower levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) of $0.0262/kWh and 4.8% higher cumulative power generation than conventional modules.
“We argue that wide-bandgap materials represented by ZnO are not limited to HJT cells; through doping modulation, interface engineering, and optimization of film deposition processes, they can be further extended to TOPCon, perovskite, and perovskite-silicon tandem cells, serving as efficient UV-absorbing layers and interfacial stabilization layers with broad application potential,” Yu stated. “With increasingly stringent requirements for long-term weatherability in high-efficiency photovoltaic devices, we believe that wide-bandgap metal oxides will demonstrate extensive application prospects in all mainstream solar cell systems by virtue of its excellent optical properties and interface compatibility.”
The research findings are available in “
Suppressing UV-induced degradation of silicon solar cells and modules by UV-cutoff zinc oxide films
,” published in
Current Applied Physics

title: South Korea selects first villages for community solar scheme - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The Sunshine Income Villages scheme plans to deploy solar installations across South Korea under a resident-led renewable energy profit-sharing model.
Patrick Jowett
10 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Residential
South Korea
Image: Stephanie Nakagawa/Unsplash
The South Korean government has selected the first 86 villages to take part in its Sunshine Income Villages initiative.
First unveiled earlier this year, the scheme aims to install solar power facilities on idle land, farmland and reservoirs, with local residents forming cooperatives to participate in the projects via energy and profit sharing.
The 86 villages were chosen from 129 that applied during the first open call for participants. A further 34 were recommended to reapply during the second call, which wrapped up at the end of July.
According to an update posted by the country’s Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment (MCEE), nine of the approved villages were assessed as capable of rapid project implementation as they already meet all business requirements, such as established financial plans, secure site selection and the formation of a cooperative.
The remaining 77 selected applicants are referred to as ‘conditionally selected’ as some of the necessary requirements for participation in the scheme, such as financial plans, grid connections and lease negotiations, are yet to be finalized.
MCEE’s update says the government will now “promptly guide the selected villages through follow-up procedures”, including grant permits and providing financial support covering up to 85% of solar installation costs.
South Korea’s Minister of Interior and Safety, Yoon Ho-joong, said he expects the 86 Sunshine Income Villages selected in this first round of applications to “become exemplary cases and serve as a stepping stone for nationwide expansion.”
“As many villages from all over the region have applied for the second round of applications, we will cooperate closely with relevant ministries to do our best to ensure that as many villages as possible are selected and can enjoy the benefits,” he added.
In its second search for participants, the government received 617 village applications from 116 cities and counties across 12 provinces and cities nationwide. Final selection results are expected at the end of September.
The Ministry of Interior and Safety has set a target of identifying 700 solar villages this year, increasing to 2,500 by 2030.
Reports in South Korean media add that the government is currently in discussions to add an energy systems support scheme program to complement the Sunlight Income Villages initiative, particularly in areas with limited grid capacity.
Last week, a groundbreaking ceremony took place for South Korea’s
largest single-site PV complex
to date. In July, the country announced its latest solar tender covering
1 GW of new solar capacity
South Korea’s cumulative solar capacity reached 30,346 MW by the end of 2025, according to figures published by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), a 3.6 GW increase on data reported at the end of 2024.

title: European transmission system operators prepare for solar eclipse - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
European transmission system operators are preparing for the August 12 solar eclipse, which is expected to temporarily reduce photovoltaic generation but pose no threat to electricity supply. French and German grid operators forecast PV output declines of around 9.7 GW and 2 GW, respectively, with the impact expected to be lower than during previous eclipses.
Sandra Enkhardt,
François Puthod
10 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
O eclipse solar parcial de março de 2025 transcorreu sem incidentes. Os operadores dos sistemas de transmissão esperam o mesmo para o evento de 12 de agosto. | Imagem: pv magazine/ Sandra Enkhardt
Europe will see a solar eclipse on August 12, with a total eclipse visible along a narrow path and a partial eclipse across much of the continent. As the moon passes between the sun and Earth, solar irradiance will temporarily decline, reducing photovoltaic generation in affected areas.
The impact will vary across countries depending on the degree of solar obscuration, weather conditions, and installed PV capacity. Transmission system operators across Europe are preparing for the temporary reduction in solar power feed-in, but do not expect the event to threaten the security of electricity supply.
German transmission system operators 50Hertz, Amprion, TenneT, and TransnetBW said on Friday that they are preparing for the event together with their European partners. Photovoltaic generation is expected to decline earlier than it would on a typical summer evening. However, the extent of the reduction remains uncertain and will depend largely on cloud cover.
The German transmission system operators forecast a reduction of around 2 GW in photovoltaic generation. Given Germany’s installed photovoltaic capacity of 125 GW, they said the lower output will not affect the country’s electricity supply on Wednesday.
The European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity (ENTSO-E) has also established a working group to prepare for the solar eclipse. The situation is being continuously assessed, and measures can be initiated at short notice if necessary. However, no impact on the security of electricity supply is expected, including at the European level.
French grid operator RTE forcasts that, under clear-sky conditions, French photovoltaic output could fall by around 1,800 MW, while European PV generation could decline by nearly 9,700 MW at the peak of the eclipse, between 7:30 p.m. and 9:30 p.m. These reductions are lower than those recorded during the eclipses in 2015 and 2025, while the timing is also favorable, as the event will occur before nightfall.
The partial solar eclipse on March 20, 2015, caused photovoltaic generation in France to fall by around 2,000 MW, while the decline across Europe reached nearly 35 GW. Thanks to careful preparation and coordination among transmission system operators across Europe through ENTSO-E, the grid was operated without difficulty in real time.
The partial solar eclipse in 2021 confirmed the effectiveness of the methods put in place, with a more limited impact of around 550 MW in France. During the most recent solar eclipse visible in France, in 2025, the mobilization of grid operators and advance planning measures once again ensured uninterrupted grid operations. Each event has helped refine the forecasting methods and grid management procedures used today.

title: France expands renewable curtailment mechanism amid negative prices, lowers threshold to 1 MW - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
France will expand its renewable curtailment mechanism to more solar and wind installations, lowering the capacity threshold from 10 MW to 1 MW in two stages from December 2026. The rules target periods of negative electricity prices, with EDF preparing affected operators for remote shutdowns while maintaining existing compensation arrangements.
